verses.text: In those days, the Philistines gathered their armies together for warfare, to fight with Israel. Achish said to David, “Know assuredly that you will go out with me in the army, you and your men.”
David said to Achish, “Therefore you will know what your servant can do.” Achish said to David, “Therefore I will make you my bodyguard forever.”
Now Samuel was dead, and all Israel had mourned for him, and buried him in Ramah, even in his own city. Saul had put away those who had familiar spirits the wizards, out of the land.
The Philistines gathered themselves together, and came and encamped in Shunem; and Saul gathered all Israel together, and they encamped in Gilboa.
When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
When Saul inquired of Yahweh, Yahweh didn’t answer him by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets.

Then Saul said to his servants, “Seek for me a woman who has a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and inquire of her.” His servants said to him, “Behold, there is a woman who has a familiar spirit at Endor.”

Saul disguised himself and put on other clothing, and went, he and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night. Then he said, “Please consult for me by the familiar spirit, and bring me up whomever I shall name to you.”

The woman said to him, “Behold, you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off those who have familiar spirits, and the wizards, out of the land. Why then do you lay a snare for my life, to cause me to die?”
Saul swore to her by Yahweh, saying, “As Yahweh lives, no punishment will happen to you for this thing.”
Then the woman said, “Whom shall I bring up to you?” He said, “Bring Samuel up for me.”
When the woman saw Samuel, she cried with a loud voice; and the woman spoke to Saul, saying, “Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul!”
The king said to her, “Don’t be afraid! What do you see?” The woman said to Saul, “I see a god coming up out of the earth.”
He said to her, “What does he look like?” She said, “An old man comes up. He is covered with a robe.” Saul perceived that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground, and showed respect.

Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me, to bring me up?” Saul answered, “I am very distressed; for the Philistines make war against me, and God has departed from me, and answers me no more, by prophets, or by dreams. Therefore I have called you, that you may make known to me what I shall do.”
Samuel said, “Why then do you ask me, since Yahweh has departed from you and has become your adversary?
Yahweh has done to you as he spoke by me. Yahweh has torn the kingdom out of your hand, and given it to your neighbor, even to David.
Because you didn’t obey Yahweh’s voice, and didn’t execute his fierce wrath on Amalek, therefore Yahweh has done this thing to you today.

Moreover Yahweh will deliver Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines; and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. Yahweh will deliver the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines.”
Then Saul fell immediately his full length on the earth, and was terrified, because of Samuel’s words. There was no strength in him; for he had eaten no bread all day long or all night long.

The woman came to Saul, and saw that he was very troubled, and said to him, “Behold, your servant has listened to your voice, and I have put my life in my hand, and have listened to your words which you spoke to me.
Now therefore, please listen also to the voice of your servant, and let me set a morsel of bread before you. Eat, that you may have strength, when you go on your way.”
But he refused, and said, “I will not eat.” But his servants, together with the woman, constrained him; and he listened to their voice. So he arose from the earth and sat on the bed.
The woman had a fattened calf in the house. She hurried and killed it; and she took flour, and kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread of it.
She brought it before Saul, and before his servants; and they ate. Then they rose up, and went away that night.

footnotes.content: The Philistines gather for war—and David, who has been fleeing Saul, is now caught between two loyalties. Achish trusts him completely. In our own crisis, we often find ourselves in places we never expected, tested in ways we couldn't predict. But the Lord sees and is already at work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's words sound obedient, yet he is hedging—saying Achish will know what his servant can do without naming what that truly is. How gently the Lord sometimes holds us through our evasions, all while working His own purposes. Even our half-answers sometimes land in His hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel is dead, mourned fully by all Israel. Yet Saul, who once had the great prophet's counsel, had removed the mediums and wizards from the land—the right command, done for the right reason. But now, stripped of prophetic voice, he will seek them out in secret. Obedience abandoned becomes desperation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shunem and Gilboa—place names that mark the stage where kingship itself is about to be judged. Shunem belonged to the tribe of Issachar. The geography speaks: Israel is massed against an enemy who will win the day. When we gather our strength and find ourselves still outmatched, we learn what we truly trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul is afraid. His heart trembles. This is not weakness alone—this is a man who once had God's Spirit, who once moved with confidence, now sensing that he stands alone. Fear whispers that we are abandoned. But fear is not the final word; it is sometimes the first step toward seeking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul inquires of the Lord—dreams, Urim, prophets—and hears nothing. Silence from God is its own answer, but oh, how hard silence is to bear. The Lord's refusal to speak does not mean He is indifferent; it means this king has exhausted the means by which he might hear truth. Now he will seek lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul turns to his servants: Find me a medium. He is no longer the king enforcing the law but a fugitive from his own commandments. Yet notice—his servants know exactly where to find one. Evil waits nearby, patient, for the moment we decide to reach for it instead of the One who has not yet let go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul disguises himself. A king, hiding his face, seeking counsel in darkness at night. His need has made him someone he never imagined becoming. Yet we have all disguised our truest self at some point, hoping no one—and perhaps hoping God—would notice. He always does, and still He waits.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The woman suspects a trap. She knows Saul has hunted people like her—and she is right to fear. But in that moment, do we hear a whisper of her own conscience? She has a trade in secret counsel, yet she fears the king who would judge her. Some part of her knows what she does is wrong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul swears by Yahweh—"As Yahweh lives"—while asking her to do the very thing the Lord forbids. The irony cuts deep. We invoke God's name to help us disobey Him. Yet even in that contradiction, the Lord remains sovereign over His own name and His own purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bring Samuel up for me. Saul asks her to summon the only voice he ever truly trusted. In his desperation, he reaches backward for a prophet who is dead rather than forward toward the Living God who still speaks. Grief, fear, and pride have tangled into a knot he cannot untie.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The woman cries out with recognition. Something appears—something real enough that she is terrified—and she knows who Saul is beneath his disguise. Her own art has exposed him. The Lord allows evil to advance only so far; He sets bounds even to deception.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She sees a god—an elohim—rising from the earth. Whether this was Samuel's shade or a deception, the text remains reverent about what happened. What appears is real enough to Saul that he recognizes it. The Lord permits boundaries even to the spirit world, and all that appears serves His purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An old man covered with a robe—the figure recalls Samuel as he lived. Saul's recognition is immediate and certain. He bows deeply, showing honor. Even here, in this forbidden place, Saul does homage to the memory of the one man who truly loved him. Memory itself can humble us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why have you disturbed me?" The figure's first words are stern. Saul pours out his heart—distressed, abandoned by God, without answer from prophets or dreams. He is confessing, at last, what he has known for a long time: he is truly alone. Confession, even in desperation, can be the beginning of seeing clearly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why do you ask me, since Yahweh has departed from you?" The question cuts to the heart: there is no secret counsel that can undo the Lord's judgment. Saul sought a workaround, a back door, a whisper in the dark. But there is none. The Lord's mind, once set against us, cannot be circumvented by clever seeking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The kingdom is torn from your hand and given to David. This is not new news to Saul—Samuel spoke this long ago—but to hear it again from the grave, from the one voice he trusted most, makes it irrevocable. Sometimes we need to hear the truth twice, once in hope and again in finality, before we accept it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You didn't obey about Amalek—the old wound is named. One disobedience, rooted in pride and pity mixed together, spiraled into a lifetime of alienation from God. Saul's fall was not one moment but one choice made long ago and never truly repented of. The heart remembers what the mind tries to forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. Death is announced not as mercy but as the end of the trial. Yet there is also a strange reversal: Saul feared abandonment, and now he is told he will be "with" Samuel. Even in judgment, the Lord does not leave His people utterly alone. Comfort and terror are sometimes one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul falls—his full length on the earth. He is terrified, emptied of strength, having eaten nothing all day. His body mirrors his soul: collapsed, undone, waiting. In the moment of final truth, resistance ends. The Lord sometimes must break us completely before He can restore us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The woman comes to him, no longer afraid but moved to compassion. She has risked her life for him; now she pleads that he live. She sees him broken and acts with mercy. Sometimes the Lord's kindness comes through unexpected hands—hands we thought opposed us. Grace has strange couriers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Eat, that you may have strength." The woman urges life into the dying king. She has served him the only gift she has left—a meal, offered with her own hands. After darkness, after judgment, after collapse, she offers bread. The simplest mercies often come when we least deserve them and most need them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He refuses; his servants and the woman constrain him. Even in defeat, Saul resists—yet this time, resistance yields. He is persuaded to sit, to eat, to live one more day. We are sometimes saved not by our own will but by the gentle force of others who love us enough to insist that we go on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fattened calf slaughtered in haste, flour kneaded by her own hands, unleavened bread baked quickly. She spends her own wealth to feed him. The detail recalls Abraham's hospitality to the Lord—how the best was offered to a stranger in need. In caring for the broken king, this woman echoes the Lord's own lavish mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: even at the edge of judgment, a cup is offered, a table is set, and the condemned are given a final meal. In that mercy toward Saul, we glimpse the God who will one day set a table before His own in the presence of their enemies, and call them to eat and be satisfied.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
